newsitem.title: PERU: Peru government, rebels prepare for fresh talks.
newsitem.headline: Peru government, rebels prepare for fresh talks.

text.p: Peruvian officials and Marxist guerrillas were poised on Tuesday for new face-to-face hostage talks as President Alberto Fujimori blamed police for failing to foil the rebels' raid on the Japanese ambassador's home 70 days ago.
"We cannot speak about culpability yet. But there is responsibility on the part of some officials and of members of the National Police," Fujimori told reporters on Monday.

An investigation was underway, he added, and news reports said some authorities may be punished for the Dec. 17 takeover of the mansion, where Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels still hold 72 men hostage.
On Monday, government negotiator Domingo Palermo and rebel leader Nestor Cerpa agreed to hold a sixth round of face-to-face talks on Tuesday aimed at ending the standoff. No starting time was given.
A statement issued by guarantors overseeing the talks said after Monday's fifth round that the two had met in a "cordial atmosphere" and broached "important issues."

Fujimori, speaking on a trip to the eastern jungle town of Mazamari, said talks were still in a "preliminary stage" with the two sides yet to reach an accord for formal negotiations to end the crisis.

The president also said Peru's intelligence service had informed police weeks before the takeover that MRTA rebels had sent weapons and fighters from the central jungle to the capital for a hostage-taking operation.
Police high command ordered preventive steps on Nov. 15 but, "apparently, adequate measures were not taken to assure that the reception at the Japanese embassy take place normally," he added.

His comments confirmed a secret police report obtained by Reuters that showed regional anti-terrorist police in mid-October had warned authorities in Lima that the MRTA was planning an assault around Nov. 30.
Guerrillas seized the diplomatic compound in a spectacular assault, taking hostage hundreds of VIP cocktail party guests. Most have been released.
After weeks of intransigence over the main rebel demand of freedom for some 400 jailed comrades, face-to-face talks to end the crisis restarted on Feb. 11.

Fujimori, meanwhile, denied a Japanese newspaper's report that he had agreed to place on the agenda for final negotiations the main MRTA demand of freedom for jailed rebels, something the government has flatly rejected from the start.
"The government's position is the same," he said.

A leading expert on Peru's guerrilla wars told local radio on Tuesday he was optimistic for a peaceful end to the crisis, adding Cerpa was unlikely to insist on freedom for jailed rebel leaders for fear of losing gains the MRTA has already made.
"For Cerpa to propose freedom for (rebel chiefs Victor) Polay and Peter Cardenas would seem contrary to his behaviour until now," Carlos Tapia told Radioprogramas del Peru

After Monday's meeting, Cerpa and his deputy, Rolly Rojas, were driven back to the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence in a Red Cross car from a safe house across the street where the talks are being held.

When they left the diplomatic compound earlier in the morning, their fellow rebels cheered, broadcast a revolutionary anthem commemorating dead comrades and bellowed defiant slogans. "We are the ones who have taken the Japanese residence. Until death, damn it!" they shouted.
Argentine human rights group Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo, meanwhile, were rebuffed again on Monday in their bid to play a role in resolving the hostage crisis.

A Mothers delegation was turned away at Government Palace when they tried for a second time to meet with Fujimori and were barred from visiting a women's prison as well as paying a visit to the hostages. They vowed to try again on Tuesday.
